records.title: Source
records.purpose: Source is the project's zero-point: the conceptual condition from which distinction, relationship and manifestation begin. It is not merely the first word in the ontology. It is the question beneath every origin story: before there are Father and Son, heaven and earth, garden and house, what is being treated as prior? In the project, Source therefore operates at several levels at once: theological language about God as origin, philosophical questions about first principles, narrative architecture, and an analytical placeholder for what a system assumes before it starts dividing reality into parts.
records.context: Biblical language repeatedly uses origin language for God and creation. Genesis 1 begins with God creating heaven and earth; John 1 describes the Word as being with God and participating in creation; Colossians 1:16-17 describes all things as created through and held together in Christ. These passages belong to different theological texts and traditions and should not be collapsed into one technical doctrine. They do, however, provide a rich textual field for studying origin, dependence, creation and coherence.
mechanisms: provides a reference point for differentiation
allows the archive to ask what is assumed before analysis begins
creates a relation from origin to manifestation rather than treating objects as self-explanatory
connects mythic language to questions of emergence, dependence and first principles
questions: Is Source being used as theology, metaphysics, narrative device or analytical placeholder?
What changes when the assumed origin changes?
If everything downstream depends upon Source, what does dependence actually mean?
Can an origin remain conceptually present after a system becomes complex?
failure_modes: Treating a symbolic origin as an empirical discovery
Using Source to end an investigation rather than begin one
Pretending different religious accounts of origin say exactly the same thing
Confusing chronological firstness with ontological dependence
records.use_in_project: Source belongs above the filing tree because it is an interpretive starting condition. It should connect downward into every later layer rather than become an isolated keyword.
records.transcendence: The deeper reading is that Source is not necessarily one more object sitting behind all other objects. It can represent the limit reached when the mind asks what makes any distinction possible at all. Source therefore becomes a boundary between explanation and the question of why there is a world capable of being explained.

records.title: Father
records.purpose: Father is the upper/source-side role in the project's mythology. Its analytical value is relational: Father becomes intelligible through Source, Son, House, Garden, Heaven, authority, generation, inheritance and return. Rather than treating Father as a generic synonym for God, the archive studies what the father image does inside biblical language and inside the project's own symbolic architecture. Father represents origin expressed as relationship: the source is imagined not merely as an abstract principle but as one who gives, knows, sends, receives, houses and restores.
records.context: The Hebrew Bible contains many uses of father-language for God, Israel's ancestors and human relationships. In the New Testament, Jesus' teaching frequently speaks of 'the Father'; the Lord's Prayer begins with 'Our Father' (Matthew 6:9), while John develops an unusually strong Father-Son relational vocabulary. The parable of the prodigal son (Luke 15:11-32) is especially important for this project because the father is encountered not simply as authority but as one who waits, receives, restores relationship and gives the household back to the returning child. Isaiah 64:8 uses the potter/father image for God and Israel; Psalm 103:13 compares divine compassion to a father's compassion for children.
mechanisms: represents origin and organizing authority inside the myth
creates a vertical and relational relation to the Son
turns abstract source-language into a household relationship
provides a symbolic counterpoint to embodiment and return
allows authority to be studied as care, generation, inheritance and responsibility rather than domination alone
questions: What does Father give, and what does the Son receive?
How does authority differ from control in the biblical texts?
Why does household language become a vehicle for transcendence?
How does the Father's relationship to the Son change through death, absence, return and recognition?
failure_modes: Turning a project mythic role into a claim about real-world political authority
Reducing Father to a generic synonym for God
Assuming fatherhood automatically means domination
Ignoring the diversity of biblical uses of father-language
records.use_in_project: Father should be displayed as a dense relational record. Opening Father should immediately expose its links to Source, Son, House, Garden, Heaven and the biblical passages that make those relationships intelligible.
records.transcendence: At the deepest level, Father can be read as the transformation of 'origin' into 'relationship'. The question stops being merely 'what caused the world?' and becomes 'what kind of relation could sustain what comes from the source?' That movement from cause to relationship is central to the project's architecture.

records.title: Garden
records.purpose: Garden is the image of a bounded world in which life is cultivated, differentiated and entrusted to living beings. It is not simply 'nature' and not simply a paradise. A garden implies soil, water, boundaries, work, growth, naming, relationship, vulnerability and stewardship. In Genesis, Eden is both abundance and responsibility: the human is placed within it to work and keep it, while the story introduces knowledge, prohibition, desire, rupture, hiding and exile. The garden therefore becomes a bridge between Source and House: it is created space before it becomes organized domestic space.
records.context: Genesis 2:8-15 describes God planting a garden in Eden and placing the human there to work and keep it. Genesis 3 turns the garden into the scene of transgression, hiding and expulsion. Ezekiel 28:13 uses Eden as symbolic imagery, while Isaiah 51:3 later uses garden language for restoration. In the New Testament, Jesus is arrested in a garden (John 18:1) and Mary Magdalene encounters the risen Jesus near a garden/tomb setting (John 20), allowing garden imagery to appear at both the beginning and resurrection end of a biblical narrative arc.
mechanisms: creates a living environment rather than an empty container
joins material ground to cultivation and meaning
establishes boundaries and responsibilities
turns abundance into something that can be tended or damaged
provides a recurring setting for innocence, rupture, burial and renewal
questions: What is the difference between a garden and wilderness in the symbolic system?
Why does cultivation require both freedom and boundaries?
What is lost when a garden becomes merely a possession?
Can restoration mean returning to the original garden, or creating a transformed one?
failure_modes: Reducing Eden to a literal map location without engaging the text's literary and theological layers
Treating nature as automatically harmonious
Assuming cultivation means domination
Using paradise language to erase the labour and limits present in the garden story
records.use_in_project: Garden is a major connector between creation, matter, life, responsibility and restoration. It should not be left as a one-word entry.
records.transcendence: The deeper reading of Garden is that transcendence may begin not by leaving matter but by learning how to inhabit matter differently. The sacred space is cultivated ground: soil becomes place, place becomes relationship, relationship becomes responsibility, and responsibility becomes a possible form of return.

records.title: Father's House
records.purpose: Father's House is the project's central dwelling metaphor for origin experienced as belonging. It represents the place from which the Son comes, the place to which return is possible, and the interior order in which many rooms can coexist without becoming identical. The image is deliberately architectural because architecture makes relationship visible: a house has an outside and inside, threshold and rooms, foundations and roof, private and shared spaces. In the project's mythology, Father's House therefore joins Source to embodiment through a spatial metaphor of belonging and return.
records.context: John 14:2 is the key biblical reference: Jesus speaks of 'my Father's house' and 'many rooms' in the context of preparing a place for the disciples. The wording has generated substantial translation and interpretive discussion; some translations render the Greek term as rooms, dwelling places or mansions. The important project point is not to force one English rendering but to preserve the architectural image of a household containing multiple places. Hebrews 3:4-6 also uses house imagery, distinguishing the builder of a house from the house itself and placing Moses and Christ within a broader argument about God's household.
mechanisms: creates an interior model of belonging
organizes many differentiated spaces around a common source
connects departure and return
turns transcendence into a spatial relationship rather than an abstract location
allows individual identity to persist within a larger unity
questions: What does it mean for a house to contain many rooms without becoming fragmented?
Is the house a destination, a relationship, a state of belonging, or all three in different readings?
What makes a room part of the Father's House?
How does the threshold between outside and inside relate to Door and Son?
failure_modes: Treating the house as a literal astronomical structure
Assuming 'many rooms' proves a specific afterlife geography
Collapsing different translations into a single unquestionable wording
Confusing belonging with possession
records.use_in_project: Father's House should be one of the project's dense anchor records. It should visibly open into Father → House → Rooms/Mansions → Heaven and into Son → Door → Return.
records.transcendence: The house becomes more than a place when 'inside' means participation in a relationship. A room does not need to be identical to another room to belong to the same house. This offers a deeper model of unity: unity is not sameness but coordinated belonging around a shared source.

records.title: House
records.purpose: House is the broader architectural pattern underlying Father's House. It represents organized dwelling: a boundary that separates inside from outside while creating differentiated spaces within. Unlike a single container, a house contains relationships between rooms, entrances, corridors, foundations, thresholds and inhabitants. It is therefore an unusually useful metaphor for the repository itself: the archive can be thought of as a house in which records are rooms, navigation is the corridor system, the ontology is the structural frame, and relationships are doors between spaces.
records.context: House imagery is widespread in the Bible. Joshua 24:15 speaks of a household choosing whom it will serve. 2 Samuel 7 uses house language for David's dynasty as well as physical dwelling. Proverbs repeatedly uses household architecture as wisdom imagery. Jesus speaks of a house built on rock in Matthew 7:24-27. Paul uses the household of God in 1 Timothy 3:15 and the household metaphor in Ephesians 2:19. These uses show that 'house' can describe architecture, family, institution, dynasty and community without becoming reducible to any one of them.
mechanisms: separates but also connects spaces
provides stable structure for changing inhabitants
creates thresholds and levels of access
allows private, shared and sacred spaces to coexist
turns abstract community into a spatially legible system
questions: What makes a collection of rooms a house rather than a pile of rooms?
Where is the threshold between private and common space?
What are the foundations of a symbolic house?
When does architecture become institution?
failure_modes: Treating metaphorical architecture as literal geography
Assuming order always means hierarchy
Forcing every concept into a room
Ignoring people and relationships in favour of structure
records.use_in_project: House should become a reusable structural concept across the atlas, connecting architecture, family, institution, archive and metaphysical dwelling.
records.transcendence: A house is an answer to the problem of how unity can contain difference. Its deeper question is not 'where is heaven?' but 'what kind of structure could allow many distinct lives to belong to one whole without erasing their distinction?'

records.title: Rooms
records.purpose: Rooms are differentiated places within a common house. They make the project's notion of unity more precise because a house can contain many rooms without requiring every room to have the same function. A room may be private, shared, transitional, ceremonial, practical or hidden. In the project's symbolic architecture, rooms therefore model differentiated states of being, domains of knowledge and individual forms of belonging within Father's House.
records.context: John 14:2 provides the central reference through the phrase traditionally translated as 'many mansions' and, in many modern translations, 'many rooms'. The Greek noun monai can be understood in terms of dwelling places or abiding places. The textual issue matters because the project should preserve the source language and translation history instead of treating one English word as the entire meaning.
mechanisms: differentiates functions inside unity
provides local identity without severing common belonging
creates paths and thresholds between domains
allows complexity to remain ordered rather than flattened
questions: Are rooms states, places, persons, traditions, domains or metaphors?
What connects one room to another?
Can a room change function while remaining part of the same house?
What happens when a room becomes isolated from the rest of the house?
failure_modes: Turning rooms into a rigid hierarchy of spiritual ranks
Assuming every room corresponds to a specific literal place
Using multiplicity as an excuse for incoherence
Treating difference as separation
records.use_in_project: Rooms should be connected to repository branches and domains as an analogy, while remaining distinct from the actual filing taxonomy.
records.transcendence: The room metaphor offers a subtle model of plurality: the whole can be larger than any one perspective without making the perspectives meaningless. A room is a local view of a larger house. The challenge is to preserve the local view while keeping the path back to the whole.

records.title: Mansions / Dwelling Places
records.purpose: Mansions is retained because it is historically important to the project's English-language symbolic vocabulary, while the record explicitly distinguishes the traditional translation from the broader sense of the underlying biblical language. The point is not to claim that heaven contains luxury houses. The image can instead be studied as an expanding dwelling metaphor: permanence, belonging, prepared space and participation in a household.
records.context: John 14:2 is central. Older English traditions commonly use 'mansions', while many contemporary translations use 'rooms' or 'dwelling places'. This variation is itself useful evidence: translation choices can reshape the symbolic imagination. The project should therefore show the English history alongside the underlying text and interpretive questions rather than presenting 'mansions' as a simple architectural fact.
mechanisms: converts dwelling into an image of permanence
creates a prepared-place motif
connects individual dwelling with a larger household
demonstrates how translation changes symbolic emphasis
questions: What did 'mansion' communicate in older English that 'room' communicates differently today?
How much of the popular image comes from translation rather than the Greek text?
Does permanence mean physical permanence or relational permanence?
failure_modes: Reading modern luxury-house meanings back into ancient texts
Treating translation as if it were the original language
Building an afterlife geography from one metaphor
records.use_in_project: Mansions is a useful cross-link from biblical language to translation history and then back into the project's House/Rooms architecture.
records.transcendence: The strongest interpretation may be that what is 'prepared' is not a luxury object but a place in a relationship. The mansion becomes an image for enduring belonging rather than material wealth.

records.title: Heaven
records.purpose: Heaven is the project's symbolic upper domain of integration, clarity, relationship and love. It is not treated as a geographic location that the archive has empirically mapped. Biblical heaven-language is plural and layered: sky, created heavens, divine dwelling, God's sovereignty, eschatological hope and symbolic contrast with earth can overlap without being identical. The project therefore uses Heaven as a coordinate in its mythic architecture while preserving the difference between scriptural imagery, theological interpretation and physical cosmology.
records.context: Genesis 1 distinguishes the heavens and the earth. Psalm 19 uses the heavens as testimony to creation. Matthew's Gospel frequently uses 'kingdom of heaven' language. Isaiah 66:1 describes heaven as God's throne and earth as his footstool, shifting attention away from heaven as a normal physical residence. Revelation 21-22 describes a renewed creation in which divine dwelling is associated with humanity and the holy city, complicating a simple picture of souls escaping earth. John 14 links the Father's House to prepared dwelling places. These texts together make Heaven a much richer subject than 'place above'.
mechanisms: provides an imagined endpoint of coherence
contrasts fragmented lower conditions with an ordered whole
organizes symbolic language around presence, sovereignty, relationship and return
allows eschatological renewal to be distinguished from simple escape
questions: Is heaven being described as place, presence, order, relationship, kingdom, future condition or symbol?
Why do biblical texts sometimes move from heaven-above imagery toward renewed creation?
What would 'heaven on earth' mean without reducing heaven to politics or comfort?
Can transcendence preserve matter rather than reject it?
failure_modes: Confusing symbolic heaven with astronomical location
Treating moral hierarchy as a physical coordinate
Reducing diverse biblical heaven-language to one doctrine
Assuming transcendence necessarily means leaving the material world
records.use_in_project: Heaven is a mythic coordinate above the Plane, but it should link downward into Garden, House, Son, Door and renewed World rather than remain a floating endpoint.
records.transcendence: The deeper movement in the biblical material is potentially from 'above' to 'within and among'. Heaven can represent not merely another place but a different mode of relation: source and creation reconciled, fragmented things integrated, and dwelling restored. That allows transcendence to mean transformation of the relationship to existence rather than simple escape from existence.

records.title: Ladder
records.purpose: The Ladder turns vertical difference into a route. It is more useful than a static hierarchy because it implies movement, effort, intermediate states and the possibility of descent as well as ascent. Genesis 28 gives the project its central biblical image: Jacob sees a ladder/stairway between earth and heaven, with angels ascending and descending. The image therefore already contains two-way movement, communication and connection rather than merely a ladder upward.
records.context: Genesis 28:10-17 is the primary reference. Jesus echoes Jacob's image in John 1:51 when he speaks of heaven opened and angels ascending and descending upon the Son of Man. This creates an important project coupling: Ladder → Son → Door/threshold → Heaven. The archive should distinguish the biblical texts from the project's later dimensional metaphors.
mechanisms: orders stages
makes transitions legible
connects otherwise separated levels
allows descent as well as ascent
turns a hierarchy into a process
questions: What does each rung measure?
What evidence would justify a transition between levels?
Why does biblical ladder imagery include descent?
Can transformation occur sideways as well as vertically?
failure_modes: Assuming higher automatically means morally better
Inventing levels without definitions
Turning symbolic dimensions into physics
Ignoring descent, return and embodiment
records.use_in_project: The Ladder is a transformation model for both mythic architecture and navigation, but it must not be mistaken for an empirical measurement unless a measurement is supplied.
records.transcendence: The ladder becomes a model for translation between orders of experience. Its deepest value is not the top rung but the existence of a relationship between otherwise separated domains.

records.title: Narrow Gate
records.purpose: The Narrow Gate represents a threshold with constraints. It makes the project's Door metaphor more specific: transformation is not simply movement but movement under conditions. Matthew 7:13-14 and Luke 13:24 use narrowness to describe a demanding way. The image can therefore be coupled to Door, Son and Vessel without claiming that the biblical passage is a technical diagram of dimensions.
records.context: Matthew 7:13-14 contrasts the broad way with the narrow gate and difficult way. Luke 13:24 similarly speaks of striving to enter through the narrow door. The vocabulary supports a project reading of threshold, constraint, decision and transformation, while the theological meaning must remain anchored in the text.
mechanisms: limits passage
forces selection
creates distinction between states
makes transformation costly or demanding in the narrative
questions: What is excluded by the gate?
What must be relinquished to pass?
Is narrowness about scarcity, commitment, discipline or perception?
How does the gate relate to the person who passes through it?
failure_modes: Using difficulty as proof of truth
Turning a symbolic threshold into a literal supernatural mechanism
Using the narrow gate to justify exclusion of real people
Ignoring the ethical context of the passage
records.use_in_project: It is a transformation model, not a repository branch.
records.transcendence: The threshold can be understood as a change in the conditions under which one perceives and acts. The 'narrowness' is therefore potentially the narrowing of self-serving possibilities until a different relation becomes possible.

records.title: Vessel
records.purpose: Vessel describes the carrier that allows something to cross a boundary. In the Potatoverse it makes the Son's function concrete: the carrier is part of the transformation rather than an external observer. The metaphor also has biblical resonance because bodies, households, temples and containers can all become images for carrying, inhabiting or receiving something greater than themselves.
records.context: Biblical vessel imagery includes 2 Corinthians 4:7, where Paul speaks of treasure in jars of clay, and 2 Timothy 2:20-21, which uses vessels for differing purposes. These passages should not be treated as identical to the project's Son/Door metaphor, but they show why container language is powerful: something valuable can be carried by an apparently ordinary material form.
mechanisms: contains
protects
transports
creates an interface between origin and destination
allows an abstract or invisible relation to become embodied
questions: What is being carried?
What is changed by being carried?
Does the vessel remain the same after carrying?
Can a vessel be both container and threshold?
failure_modes: Assuming the carrier is neutral
Confusing symbolic carrying with physical transmission
Treating bodies as disposable containers
Using vessel language to deny embodiment
records.use_in_project: Vessel links Door, Son, body, interface and transformation.
records.transcendence: The vessel reverses the common assumption that transcendence requires abandoning embodiment. The container becomes the means through which something beyond the container is encountered, making embodiment itself part of the mystery rather than merely a prison.

records.title: Pineal Gland
records.purpose: The pineal gland is included as an explicit metaphor boundary. The project can use its position in the brain as imagery for an interface without claiming that neuroscience has established it as a metaphysical portal. This is an important example of how the archive should couple real anatomy to symbolic language without confusing the two.
records.context: The pineal gland is a real endocrine structure involved in melatonin production and circadian regulation. Its later philosophical and popular association with the 'seat of the soul' is especially associated with René Descartes, not with biblical anatomy. The project should preserve this history because it demonstrates how a real structure can acquire layers of metaphysical interpretation.
mechanisms: the gland is a real endocrine structure involved in melatonin regulation
the brain provides a physical substrate for perception and cognition
the metaphor maps an imagined interface onto a real anatomical object
questions: Which claims about the gland are scientific?
Which are symbolic?
Why is an interface metaphor attractive here?
How do historical metaphors become mistaken for scientific findings?
failure_modes: Pseudoscientific identification of pineal anatomy with spiritual dimensions
Using scientific vocabulary to disguise unsupported metaphysical claims
records.use_in_project: It is a test case for the project's evidence rule: real anatomy and symbolic interpretation remain separate but can be linked in the graph.
records.transcendence: The useful transcendence here is epistemic: learning to move beyond a metaphor without destroying it. A symbol can remain powerful precisely because we know it is a symbol.

records.title: Tree of Strife
records.purpose: Tree of Strife is the negative structural counterpart to Tree of Life. It models a system whose branches continue to grow while the relationships that sustain the whole become competitive, extractive or destructive. It is not a claim that conflict is inherently evil. Rather, it is a pattern for studying when growth loses reciprocity with its roots.
records.context: The project deliberately contrasts the Tree of Strife with biblical Tree of Life imagery rather than claiming that 'Tree of Strife' is a biblical term. Genesis 2-3 supplies the Tree of Life and Tree of Knowledge; Revelation 22 returns to the Tree of Life in a restored city. The project's Tree of Strife is therefore a later analytical metaphor for the opposite systemic pattern: branching without healthy integration.
mechanisms: competition redirects resources
fear narrows cooperation
extraction weakens the source
fragmentation creates isolated branches
feedback can amplify conflict
questions: Where does growth cease to regenerate its roots?
Which feedback loops turn competition into systemic damage?
What would restore reciprocal flow?
failure_modes: Treating every competition as pathological
Using the metaphor instead of identifying measurable mechanisms
records.use_in_project: It provides a systems lens for studying exploitation, fragmentation, fear and institutional decay.
records.transcendence: The tree metaphor becomes transcendent when growth is judged not by height or size alone but by whether root, branch, fruit and surrounding life remain connected. A system can become larger while becoming less alive.

records.title: Fear
records.purpose: Fear is an adaptive state that becomes analytically important when it changes decisions, relationships and institutions. It is not inherently negative; the archive studies when protection becomes control. In the symbolic layer, Fear belongs to the Tree of Strife because fear can constrict perception and make the world appear smaller, but the empirical layer must continue to study fear through psychology rather than mythology.
mechanisms: threat appraisal changes attention
avoidance reduces immediate exposure
fear can coordinate groups under danger
chronic fear can narrow exploration and increase defensive behaviour
questions: What threat is being perceived?
Is the threat proportionate to the response?
Which institutions benefit from persistent fear?
What changes when perceived risk falls?
failure_modes: Treating fear as weakness
Treating all fear as irrational
Using a consciousness scale as a substitute for psychological evidence
records.use_in_project: Fear is better studied through psychology and Hawkinscale than as a repository folder of its own.
records.transcendence: The symbolic transformation of fear is not its disappearance. It is the movement from reflexive contraction toward perception capable of holding uncertainty without immediately converting it into domination.

records.title: Anger
records.purpose: Anger is a high-energy response that can signal perceived injury, blocked goals or injustice. Its project value lies in tracking where energy becomes repair, conflict, domination or change. In the symbolic system it sits beside Fear and Strife because anger can either defend a boundary or become fuel for a destructive feedback loop.
mechanisms: appraisal identifies a violation or obstacle
arousal mobilizes action
social interpretation determines whether anger becomes protest, aggression or negotiation
feedback can escalate conflict
questions: What produced the appraisal?
What action does anger make more likely?
What converts anger into constructive change?
When does boundary protection become domination?
failure_modes: Equating anger with moral truth
Treating anger as purely destructive
Ignoring the social context that produced it
records.use_in_project: Anger belongs inside psychological/emotional frameworks and relationship graphs rather than as a separate taxonomy branch.
records.transcendence: Anger can become information without becoming command. The deeper movement is from energy as reaction to energy as discernment: something is wrong, attention is mobilized, and the next question becomes what repair would actually change the underlying condition.

records.title: Strife
records.purpose: Strife is a system condition in which relationships that could support mutual life instead produce conflict, domination or fragmentation. It is a pattern, not merely a feeling. The project uses it as a bridge between individual emotional states and large systems where incentives repeatedly turn difference into antagonism.
mechanisms: competing incentives
resource scarcity
power asymmetry
fear feedback
institutional rules that reward extraction
questions: What mechanism produces the conflict?
Who gains from the current structure?
What would change the incentives?
Which conflicts are productive and which are self-amplifying?
failure_modes: Moralizing conflict without identifying mechanisms
Treating disagreement as proof of dysfunction
records.use_in_project: Strife connects the symbolic Tree of Strife to empirical study of conflict and institutional incentives.
records.transcendence: The opposite of strife is not enforced sameness. It is a system capable of metabolizing difference without turning every difference into an existential threat.

records.title: Swamp
records.purpose: Swamp is a project metaphor for systems where many flows overlap, boundaries become difficult to see and extraction or dysfunction accumulates. It is useful precisely because it describes opacity and entanglement rather than a single villain. A swamp can contain life; the metaphor becomes negative only when the archive identifies specific mechanisms of stagnation, opacity or extraction.
mechanisms: overlapping incentives
hidden dependencies
feedback loops
information asymmetry
institutional inertia
questions: Where are the hidden flows?
Which actors benefit from opacity?
Which boundary would make the system easier to understand?
Which apparently separate problems share the same infrastructure?
failure_modes: Using Swamp as a label for real people or groups without evidence
Treating metaphorical corruption as an empirical diagnosis
records.use_in_project: Swamp should point to measurable relationships and evidence rather than replace them.
records.transcendence: The swamp becomes a useful image when the goal is not to drain everything but to understand the ecology of the system. Clarity comes from tracing flows, not from inventing a single enemy.

records.title: Mud
records.purpose: Mud is the project's ground metaphor: difficult material conditions, buried history, friction and the starting point from which growth emerges. Its value is anti-romantic: transformation does not begin in clean abstraction. The potato grows through soil; likewise, a symbolic system that forgets material conditions becomes detached from the world it claims to interpret.
mechanisms: material constraints limit options
buried dependencies remain influential
friction slows transformation
stored resources can support later growth
questions: What is underneath the visible system?
Which constraints are being ignored?
What can actually grow from this substrate?
Which apparently spiritual problem is partly material?
failure_modes: Romanticizing hardship
Treating the metaphor as geological science
Using spiritual language to avoid material causes
records.use_in_project: Mud is the symbolic bridge between Matter and the Potato of Life.
records.transcendence: Mud gives the project a material test for transcendence: if an idea cannot survive contact with embodiment, labour, scarcity, history and relationship, it may be an abstraction rather than transformation.

records.title: Drain
records.purpose: Drain describes a one-way relationship in which resources, attention, value or information leave a system without sufficient renewal. It becomes useful when the quantity and direction of the flow can be identified. The metaphor can apply to money, talent, attention, ecological resources or institutional capacity, but the archive should always specify what is actually flowing.
mechanisms: outflows exceed inflows
value is extracted without reinvestment
attention is captured by competing demands
debt service can redirect future resources
brain drain can move skills between places
questions: What is flowing out?
At what rate?
Where does it go?
What replenishes the source?
Is the outflow actually harmful, or is there reciprocal return?
failure_modes: Calling any exchange a drain
Assuming outflow is harmful without considering reciprocal returns
records.use_in_project: Drain is a graph pattern: it should become an edge with direction, quantity and provenance whenever possible.
records.transcendence: The deeper question is not simply whether something leaves, but whether the system can participate in circulation rather than depletion. Life requires flow; the problem is flow without renewal.

records.title: Fragmentation
records.purpose: Fragmentation is loss of coordination or coherence between components that still belong to the same wider system. It matters because fragmentation can increase duplication, cost and vulnerability without being visible in any one institution. The project uses it both as an empirical systems concept and as the negative counterpart to the House's ability to contain difference within a coherent whole.
mechanisms: incompatible standards
duplicated institutions
information silos
conflicting incentives
broken infrastructure links
questions: What was previously connected?
What broke the connection?
Is reintegration beneficial or would it create excessive centralization?
What is the minimum connection needed to restore function?
failure_modes: Assuming integration is always better
Confusing healthy diversity with dysfunctional fragmentation
records.use_in_project: Fragmentation is a key diagnostic for the European graph and for the Tree of Strife.
records.transcendence: The House provides the counter-image: unity can preserve rooms rather than erase them. Integration is therefore not the destruction of difference but the creation of relationships through which difference remains mutually legible.

records.title: Potatoism
records.purpose: Potatoism is the project's own interpretive framework. Its serious function is not to make ordinary objects mystical but to use the potato as a deliberately humble model for growth, memory, embodiment, humour, systems and transformation. Its value increases when every symbolic term has a function, a relationship and a clear boundary between project mythology and external evidence.
mechanisms: ordinary matter becomes a carrier of meaning
growth provides a model for development
root/fruit relations model hidden dependencies and visible outputs
humour prevents grand language from becoming self-important
the framework invites translation between symbolic and empirical layers
questions: Which claims are internal mythology and which can be tested externally?
Does the potato metaphor reveal a real relationship or merely decorate it?
What does the framework make visible that a conventional taxonomy would miss?
How do Source, Father, House, Garden, Door and Son form one coupled architecture?
failure_modes: Treating Potatoism as empirical science
Using its symbolism to bypass contradictory evidence
Adding vocabulary without giving each term a function
records.use_in_project: Potatoism is strongest when it generates questions that can be investigated in the world and when its own myths remain clearly labelled as myths.
records.transcendence: The potato is deliberately low to the ground. That makes it useful for a theory of transcendence that does not require contempt for ordinary life. The movement is not mud → heaven by abandoning mud; it is root → stem → leaf → flower/fruit and back again, a cycle in which the ordinary becomes the carrier of the extraordinary.

records.title: Spudlight
records.purpose: Spudlight names illumination emerging from grounded life. It is intentionally comic: the point is that meaning does not require abandoning ordinary material existence. The symbol belongs between Potato and Heaven because it suggests that what is 'above' can be discovered through attention to what is 'below'.
mechanisms: attention can reveal value in overlooked things
ordinary objects can become symbols
knowledge can move from obscure conditions into shared understanding
questions: What becomes visible when attention changes?
What does the metaphor reveal that literal language hides?
Can illumination remain accountable to evidence?
failure_modes: Treating symbolic light as physical energy
Using poetic language instead of explanation
records.use_in_project: Spudlight is a poetic connector between Potato, knowledge, attention and emergence.
records.transcendence: Spudlight represents a deliberately humble form of revelation: not light descending from nowhere, but understanding emerging from sustained attention to what was already present.

records.title: North Axis
records.purpose: North Axis joins symbolic orientation to geography and policy. It becomes analytically meaningful only when the symbolic North is separated from geographic north and then connected through explicit institutions, territories and relationships. It is therefore a good example of the project's general method: mythic orientation can generate a research question, but empirical relationships must carry the factual claim.
mechanisms: orientation establishes a reference direction
geography anchors the direction in actual places
networks connect territories
policy translates orientation into choices
questions: What does north mean in each context?
Which geographic and institutional relationships actually form the proposed axis?
Where does the symbolic model stop?
Which connections are measurable?
failure_modes: Treating a symbolic axis as a natural geopolitical law
Assuming geographic proximity creates political alignment
records.use_in_project: North Axis is the bridge between the project's mythic architecture and the North Programme/Economic Graph.
records.transcendence: Orientation is deeper than direction. A compass does not create the landscape; it gives movement a reference. Likewise, North can become a disciplined symbolic reference without being mistaken for a supernatural force governing geography.
